At 100% the suggestions come straight off your max.

LIB-002.text: Three rotating full-body days. The best return per hour if you train three times a week, and the easiest plan to miss a day of without derailing.

LIB-004.text: Two upper days and two lower days. More volume per muscle than full body without the six-day commitment of a full split.

LIB-006.text: The classic six-day split, run twice through. High volume and high commitment — it falls apart fast if you can only train four days.

LIB-008.text: The same split at a sustainable cadence — each day comes round once a week. A good landing spot when six days stops being realistic.

LIB-010.text: No equipment at all. Progress comes from the movement ladder — harder leverage and less assistance — rather than from adding load.

LIB-012.text: Built for one or two bells and a floor. Swings, get-ups, presses and carries, with a grip finisher on every day.

LIB-014.text: Nine weeks from not running to running five kilometres. Every run is easy — the only thing that increases is how long you go.

LIB-016.text: Eight weeks of speed work on top of an easy-running base. Assumes you can already run 5K without stopping.

LIB-019.text: Two full-body strength days and two runs a week, indefinitely. For staying strong and keeping a running base without training for anything in particular.

LIB-021.text: Twelve weeks for obstacle racing. Hills and trail instead of track, grip work on every strength day, and burpees on tired legs — because that is when they actually happen.

LIB-023.text: Twelve weeks of compromised running — the thing that actually decides a hybrid fitness race. Strength, a race simulation, intervals, and one long run each week.
